Rules:

(b) You exchange messages with the other player to agree on who gets which items. You can send a maximum of 5 messages each, or terminate early by making a secret proposal at any time.
(c) You are each asked to submit a secret proposal indicating the items you want formatted in square brackets as follows: "[Proposal: <number> <object name>, <number> <object name>, <...>]"
(d) If your proposals are complementary, i.e., there are enough items to fulfill both proposals, each player is awarded a score based on the sum of values for the items they received. Otherwise, both of you get zero points.
(e) Your goal is to maximize the score you receive.

My mistake was proposing a bundle that the opponent could not reasonably accept without giving up their high-value item. Only after confirming a verbal agreement should I submit a secret proposal that exactly matches this agreed-upon split, ensuring the proposals are complementary and both players receive a non-zero score.

I assumed that once the other player submitted a secret proposal, I could simply submit my own proposal and the game would end with a score calculation. However, the rules state that a deal is only reached if the proposals are "complementary" (i.e., they partition the set of items without overlap). Since my proposal [1 statue, 1 wrench] did not account for the remaining items (the comb and whistles) or the other player's specific proposal, the game likely ended with zero points for both. My strategy was to propose a partial allocation rather than a complete, mutually exclusive partition. Next time, I must first determine the other player's likely proposal or value function, then construct a proposal that exactly covers the remaining items to ensure complementarity. I should aim for a proposal like "[1 statue, 1 wrench, 1 comb, 1 whistle]" if I intend to take everything, or a split that leaves exactly what the other player wants, ensuring no items are left unassigned or double-counted before submitting.
